📝 Medium: https://medium.com/@ravindisandali5387

medium.titulo: How Two Developers and an AI Agent Migrated 101,000 Lines from Vue 2 to Vue 3
medium.resumo: Two years of failed attempts with LLMs, then three and a half weeks that worked. Here is the plan, the traps, and the milestones.
medium.conteudo_html:
Two years of failed attempts with LLMs, then three and a half weeks that worked. Here is the plan, the traps, and the milestones.

Klass.lk is a learning-management and institute-management platform used by tuition institutes across Sri Lanka. Teachers use it to run courses, sessions, exams, attendance, payments, and payslips. Students use it to watch lessons, pay fees, and sit papers. The frontend started in May 2021 on Vue 2 + Vuetify 2 + Vuex, and it grew as most successful products grow: one feature at a time, with few chances to stop.

By mid-2026, the frontend was 101,537 lines across 658 .vue and .js files, and two frontend developers were responsible for all of it.

Vue 2 reached end of life on 31 December 2023. Since then, every dependency upgrade was harder, every security audit was longer, and every new library we wanted came with a Vue 3-only README.

This article covers how we finally got off Vue 2. It also covers why we could not do it by hand, why the LLMs we tried from 2024 onwards did not get us there, and how the job got done in 2026 with Claude Opus 5.5 running in Claude Code.

Part 1: Why a Vue 2 → Vue 3 migration is harder than it looks

On paper, Vue 3 is “mostly compatible” with Vue 2, and that phrase is the trap. The breaking changes in Vue itself are well documented. Three things are not:

  1. your UI framework’s breaking changes, which are much larger
  2. your dependencies’ breaking changes
  3. the changes that don’t fail loudly

1. The Vue API changes

Our readiness audit counted the Vue 2-only APIs still in src/:

.native modifier                    204 sites in 118 files
custom directive hooks              7 directives, 207 call sites
.sync=                              22 sites
$set / Vue.set / $delete            18 sites
$listeners / $scopedSlots           9 sites
new Vue() instances (event shims)   8
Vuetify.framework.theme at module   12 sites

None of these is hard to change on its own. What made it hard was the scale, and how badly some of them fail.

Directive hooks are the scariest item on the list. Vue 3 renamed bind, inserted and update to beforeMount, mounted and updated. A directive object that only has the old names registers without any warning and is never called. Our v-has-permission directive removes an element when the user lacks a permission, and it is used at 131 sites. After a naive upgrade, all 131 permission-gated buttons would have rendered for every user. Lint, unit tests, and the build would all have passed. This kind of failure "fails open": nothing errors, and the protection is simply gone.

2. Vuetify 2 → Vuetify 4 is the real migration

Vue is the smaller part. For a Vuetify app, most of the work is the component library. Here is how often each component appeared:

v-list-item      725 sites   (anatomy completely rebuilt)
v-btn            627 sites   (boolean style props → variant)
v-text-field     406 sites
v-dialog         119 sites   (activator slot contract rewritten)
v-select         100 sites   (item-text → item-title)
v-data-table      46 sites   (headers, slots, pagination all changed)
v-simple-table    26 sites   (gone, becomes v-table)

In total, that came to about 2,000 edits across about 490 files, plus 177 CSS selectors in 67 files that targeted Vuetify 2’s internal class names.

The worst part is that Vuetify 4 fails by rendering something, not by throwing. Every defect we found after the swap produced a complete, plausible-looking page:

  • 218 menu activators bound no handlers. The button was there, and clicking it did nothing.
  • small was silently ignored on 364 elements, so everything rendered one size larger.
  • form.validate() Now returns a Promise. if (this.$refs.form.validate()) is always truthy, so invalid forms are submitted.
  • v-date-picker now emits a Date object. The field looked correct, but the API received the wrong shape.
  • No Vuetify 4 input emitschange, so 62 @change handlers were dead.
  • 431 typography classes matched nothing, because the type scale had been replaced.
  • Vuetify 4 changed its cascade-layer order, so the CSS reset beat every component style.

3. The dependency wall

Nine runtime dependencies were Vue 2-only, and they had to be replaced in the same commit as the framework:

@tiptap/vue-2          → @tiptap/vue-3
vue-chartjs 3 + chart.js 2  → vue-chartjs 5 + chart.js 4
vue-i18n 8             → vue-i18n 9
vuedraggable 2         → vuedraggable 4
vue2-perfect-scrollbar → vue3-perfect-scrollbar
v-viewer 1             → v-viewer 3
vue-gtag 1             → vue-gtag 2
vue-cropperjs 4        → vue-cropperjs 5
vue-pdf-embed 1        → vue-pdf-embed 2
vue-meta               → removed (one usage in the whole app)
vue-sse                → replaced with a plain EventSource
vuejs-snackbar-queue   → replaced with our own alert service

The build tooling was locked too. vite-plugin-vue2The only plugin that compiles Vue 2 single-file components supports Vite 4 at most. Vuetify 4's build plugin needs Vite 5 or later. So we could not upgrade Vite first and Vue second. Vue, Vuetify, Vite, and their plugins had to move in a single commit. We could do a lot of preparation incrementally, but not the swap itself.

Part 2: Why we couldn’t do it by hand

The numbers made the decision:

  • About 2,000 Vuetify edits, 400+ Vue API edits and 13 dependency replacements
  • A 13,707-line Vuex store full of API calls, all of which would have to be ported
  • Two frontend developers, who were shipping features at the same time: multi-currency support, discount rules, scheduled notifications and session imports all landed in the weeks around the migration
  • No test suite to tell us whether a screen still worked

A feature freeze long enough to do this by hand would have cost months of product work. A long-lived migration branch would have drifted away from master every day. And because most failures are silent, careful manual edits would still need someone to click through every screen afterwards.

The work was mostly mechanical, but it needed judgement at every site. That combination is very hard for two people to do quickly, and it seemed like exactly the job an LLM should be good at.

Part 3: Two years of trying with LLMs (2024–2025)

We didn’t start in 2026.

  • September 2024: we moved the build from Vue CLI to Vite. This one worked, and it stuck.
  • September 2024: a typescript-refactor branch was abandoned.
  • December 2024: a reactquery branch upgraded Vue to 2.7.16 and started moving data fetching to TanStack Query. The 2.7 upgrade survived. The branch was abandoned.
  • June 2025: a store-refactor branch started slimming the Vuex store. It was abandoned.

Every attempt failed in the same few ways:

Context. The models could convert one file well. They could not keep 658 files, a store and a design system in mind together. A conversion that was right for one component broke the three components that read the same store slice.

Inconsistency. Each chat session had its own approach. File 40 was converted differently from file 4, so the codebase ended up in three states at once.

No verification loop. The code compiled, and that was taken as success. As described above, compiling is the one thing a broken Vuetify 4 app still does well. Nothing in the loop ever ran the app.

No memory between sessions. Every new session started from zero, and we had to explain the codebase again. Whatever the last session had learned was lost.

The lesson was that writing the code was never the bottleneck. Planning and verification were.

Part 4: What was different with Opus 5.5

In August 2026 we tried again with Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, running as an agent against the real repository. It could read the code, run yarn lint, yarn test, yarn build and a Playwright suite, write and commit, and pick up the next session where the last one stopped.

The model was a better coder, but the bigger difference was how it organised the work.

It wrote the plan down and kept it up to date

Before it changed any code, the agent built a small set of documents in the repo. Every later session read them first:

  • CLAUDE.md: the project rules and the traps that had already bitten us. Every agent session loads it.
  • HANDOFF.md: where we are, what's done and what the next session should do. It is updated at the end of every session.
  • MIGRATION.md: how to do the work. It holds the conventions, the store-retirement procedure and the list of traps.
  • PHASE5.md: the cutover plan, including the readiness audit and its findings.
  • TYPESCRIPT.md and REVAMP.md: the follow-up work.

This solved the memory problem. A new session costs a few thousand tokens of handoff instead of re-exploring the codebase. The agent wrote the paste-in prompt for starting the next session itself:

Continue the Vue 3 / Vuetify 4 migration on klasslk-fe. Read HANDOFF.md and MIGRATION.md first, then do the next unstarted session in the plan. Do not re-derive earlier work — the handoff has the current state.

One slice per session

Sessions were kept deliberately small. While retiring the store, a session covered one domain, for example courses, payments, or exams. During the Vuetify pass, a session covered one prop or one component across the whole repo, not one screen. A rename touches the whole repo, so doing it one screen at a time leaves the code in two states at once.

A verification gate on every commit

Every commit had to pass this checklist:

1. Read HANDOFF.md + MIGRATION.md
2. Pick one prop or one component
3. Check what it became in Vuetify 4's own source — don't guess
4. Apply it, re-run the audit script — the count going down is the check
5. yarn lint && yarn test && yarn build && yarn e2e
6. Probe the change in a real browser
7. Commit, update HANDOFF.md
8. Stop. New session.

Step 4 matters more than it looks. A regex that silently matched nothing looks exactly like a regex that worked, so the agent wrote scripts/audit-vuetify-props.mjs to count the remaining Vuetify 2 props and made "count goes down" the proof. It also wrote yarn ui:compare, which loads the same screen on the new build and on production, measures the components on both, and reports where they differ. Almost every visual regression was found that way.

It built the safety net first

We had no end-to-end tests when we started, so the agent’s first milestone was a Playwright suite. Our setup has no local backend, so the suite runs against the production API, and every test is read-only by default. The one test that writes is gated behind E2E_ALLOW_WRITES.

By the end, there were 124 passing E2E tests across 49 specs and 369 unit tests. These tests caught the failures that lint, the type checker, and the build missed.

The agent also learned to check that a test is non-vacuous: break the thing the test covers and confirm the test fails. Several early tests passed against the very bug they were written to catch.

It argued with the plan when the plan was wrong

The original plan had a Phase 4: wrap every Vuetify component in our own k-* components before the swap, so the swap would be cheaper. The readiness audit showed that the wrappers used $listeners and $scopedSlots, which don't exist in Vue 3. Adopting them first meant editing about 1,300 call sites twice, with presentational changes the tests could barely verify.

The agent recommended skipping Phase 4 and wrote the argument into PHASE5.md. We accepted. Later work removed one of its two reasons, and the agent went back and recorded that too: "The decision does not flip … but the reason has narrowed. That is worth knowing if anyone reopens it."

It worked unattended, within limits

Twice we handed it the repo overnight. One instruction was “continue the migration until all the stores are migrated”. Another was “I am going to sleep, you have the session for the next five hours, continue without manual input.” 😂

It worked through the plan, committed each green slice and recorded product decisions in HANDOFF.md instead of blocking on them.

It also respected one limit that we had not spelled out. The Vue 3 + Vuetify 4 swap could not be green until most of the 2,000-edit component pass was also done. Starting the swap unattended would have traded a green tree for a red one that nobody could finish before morning. So the agent did all the preparation that could land green and explained in the handoff why it had left the swap for when we were awake.

Part 5: The milestones

The phases ran in this order:

Phase 0: Dependency and security baseline. We audited dependencies and pinned and patched them, so the swap would start from a known state.

Phase 1: Lint as a blocking gate. We got to 0 lint errors and made lint block CI.

Phase 2: The bridge layer. We added composables (useBreakpoint, useTheme, useAlerts) so that components stopped calling $vuetify directly. We also added --k-* design tokens over Vuetify's CSS variables and a small k-* component kit. The rule: never read a framework API directly from a component. Each wrapper is then the only code that changes at cutover.

Phase 3: Retire the Vuex store (26 Aug — 3 Sep 2026). We moved all server state to TanStack Vue Query: 32 query modules, one per domain. Each store slice was deleted once its last consumer had moved. The store went from 13,707 lines to 1,680, and none of what remains fetches anything. We did this before the framework swap on purpose: a deleted store slice never has to be ported, and this phase removed about 12,000 lines from the cutover.

Phase 4: Adopt the k-* kit everywhere. We skipped this phase, for the reasons above.

Phase 5: The cutover (3–6 Sep 2026). This phase had the most steps:

  • 2.0: gave all seven directives both sets of hook names, so they worked on Vue 2.7 and Vue 3. This closed the fail-open permission hole before the swap.
  • 2.1: retired $set, $delete, .sync and .native.
  • 2.2: replaced the new Vue() snackbar shims with a service.
  • 2.3: made the k-* wrappers work under either framework.
  • 2.4a: shrank the dependency wall on Vue 2.7, by dropping dead packages and replacing vue-sse with a plain EventSource. That replacement also fixed a stream leak.
  • 2.4b: the swap. Vue 3, Vuetify 4 and Vite 5 landed in one commit on 4 September.
  • 2.5: the Vuetify component pass, one prop or component at a time, across about 2,000 sites. It covered the v-model → modelValue contract, activator slots, v-list-item anatomy, data-table headers, date pickers and charts.
  • 2.6: deleted the last Vue 2.7 compatibility bridges. The migration was closed on 6 September.

After the cutover: TypeScript (7–10 Sep). We made TypeScript opt-in per file with strict on. The services, the query layer, the store, the router and main.ts are all converted, and no JavaScript is left outside components.

After that: Vuetify 4 vs production (to 20 Sep). We used ui:compare to find visual drift. Examples: form fields sat 46px apart where they used to sit 24px apart, the institute brand colour was lost, and 44 permission gates on overlay components had failed open. The branch was merged to master on 18 September.

Phase 6: UI revamp on Vuetify 4. This is in progress, one screen at a time, following REVAMP.md.

From the first store retirement to merging into master took about three and a half weeks.

Part 6: What we changed

Before:

vue 2.7.16          vuetify 2.7.2       vuex 3 (13.7k-line store)
vue-router 3        vue-i18n 8          vite 4 + vite-plugin-vue2
chart.js 2          @tiptap/vue-2       no TypeScript, no E2E

After:

vue 3.5             vuetify 4.2         @tanstack/vue-query 5 (32 modules)
vue-router 4.6      vuex 4.1 (client state only, 1.7k lines)
vue-i18n 9          vite 5 + @vitejs/plugin-vue + vite-plugin-vuetify
chart.js 4          @tiptap/vue-3       TypeScript (opt-in, strict)
vitest 2            Playwright (124 E2E tests)

Two decisions we deliberately did not take:

  • vue-router 5. It requires Vite 7+ and Pinia. Moving to Pinia is a separate decision from this migration, so we stayed on 4.6.
  • vue-i18n 11. It requires Node 22. We pinned 9.x so the migration and a Node upgrade would not be tied together.

Part 7: The traps worth knowing

If you’re planning your own migration, these are the issues that cost us the most. Each one passed lint, unit tests, and the build.

1. setup() runs before data(). A common bridge pattern is const vm = getCurrentInstance().proxy followed by computed(() => vm.page). When page is a data() field, this computed reads undefined once and never records a dependency. If you bind it to a query'senabled, the query never fires: the page renders empty, with no error. Seventeen screens shipped like this before a sweep found them all.

2. Directives on overlay components don’t run. In Vuetify 4, v-tooltip, v-menu and v-dialog render fragments, and Vue skips runtime directives on fragment roots. Our 44 v-has-permission sites on tooltip activators stopped working after the cutover. The fix was v-if="hasPermission(...)".

3. A grep for $sse matches nothing in double quotes. Ingrep "vue-sse\|\$sse", the shell turns \$ into $, and grep then reads $ as an end-of-line anchor. The agent concluded that vue-sse was unused and removed it. That broke the notification bell on every page and failed more than 90 E2E tests. Single-quote the pattern and use a bracket: grep -rn '[$]sse' src.

4. A Vuetify 2 theme write is silent in Vuetify 4. $vuetify.theme.themes.light.primary = x Writes to a key that Vuetify 4 never reads. Nothing throws, and nothing repaints, so our per-institute brand-colour picker was dead.

5. Your PDF exports will break. Vuetify 4 writes colours ascolor-mix(), and html2canvas cannot parse those. Every payslip and receipt export failed silently, because nobody had written a .catch.

6. “Mixed” is worse than “old”. Moving one screen at a time leaves the codebase speaking two dialects. Move one concept across the whole repo instead.

What the humans did

The agent did most of the typing, but not all of the work. We:

  • made the product decisions: skipping Phase 4, keeping Vuex, the target versions
  • provided the environment: E2E credentials, the 2FA seed for the super-admin suite, and production access policies
  • reviewed and merged, and checked the screens the tests could not reach
  • kept shipping features on master while the migration ran, which the agent then merged onto the Vue 3 build (23 commits in one go on 13 September)

The takeaway

Our 2024 and 2025 attempts failed, not because the models couldn’t write Vue 3. They had no memory between sessions and no way to check their own work.

In 2026, what worked was a model that treated the migration as an engineering project rather than a long series of conversions. It wrote its plan into the repo, worked in small verified slices, built the tests before it needed them, and stopped to say so when something couldn’t be done safely.

The numbers:

101,537 lines · 658 files · 2 frontend developers
766 files changed · 35,643 insertions · 27,384 deletions
Store: 13,707 → 1,680 lines
0 → 124 E2E tests, 369 unit tests
~3.5 weeks from first store retirement to master

If you have been putting off a Vue 2 app because the migration looks too big for your team, it may still be too big to do by hand. It is no longer too big to do.

Klass.lk is built by a small team in Sri Lanka. Questions about the migration are welcome in the comments.

corrida_no_ar.titulo: A luta pela ESSÊNCIA e SEGURANÇA no futuro do TRAIL RUNNING
corrida_no_ar.resumo: Entrevista com Natacha Manchado, da World Athletics, sobre o futuro e a governança do trail running. A conversa aborda o papel da federação na estruturação da modalidade, parcerias com UTMB e ITRA, regras específicas, antidoping e o potencial do Brasil no cenário internacional.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Domingo | 11 de outubro de 2026

O trail running tem crescido muito em popularidade ao redor do mundo, mas quem dita as regras e organiza a governança da modalidade? Durante o TS Summit 2026, evento organizado pela Ticket Sports, conversei com Natacha Manchado, representante brasileira na World Athletics, que tem cuidado justamente dessa área na federação internacional. Ela explicou como a entidade está se envolvendo cada vez mais com as corridas de trilha.

Segundo Natacha, o trail running é, antes de tudo, corrida, e por isso faz parte do escopo da World Athletics. A comunidade do trail muitas vezes sentia falta de um “pai e uma mãe”, uma entidade reguladora, e a federação está buscando ocupar esse espaço. O objetivo não é impor regras arbitrariamente, mas sim estruturar o esporte em conjunto com outras organizações já estabelecidas, como UTMB, ITRA e WMRA. “A gente não está concorrendo, a gente está fazendo parte desse ecossistema”, afirmou.

Um dos pontos mais importantes, segundo ela, é entender que o trail running é um “outro universo”, muito diferente da corrida de rua, e não pode ser tratado como uma simples adaptação. A modalidade exige regras específicas, principalmente por questões de segurança, como equipamentos obrigatórios. A World Athletics já possui uma regra específica para isso, a Regra 57, que trata de “Mountain and Trail Running”. Nela, há detalhes sobre o uso de celular (obrigatório para segurança, não para se filmar) e até a posição do número de peito, que precisa ser adaptada para o uso de jaquetas, por exemplo.

O sonho de ver o trail running nas Olimpíadas também foi pauta. Para Natacha, antes de pensar nisso, é preciso resolver questões fundamentais, como a unificação de um ranking global e a criação de critérios claros de qualificação para o Mundial. “Se a gente não tem isso, como vamos sonhar com Olimpíada?”, questionou. A ideia é criar um caminho lógico para os atletas de elite.

O trabalho da World Athletics também inclui um programa de certificação de provas de trail, similar aos selos (Labels) da corrida de rua, e um foco crescente no antidoping, em parceria com a Unidade de Integridade do Atletismo (AIU). Natacha citou que a Golden Trail Series já realiza os testes com a AIU, e a ideia é expandir esse controle para garantir um esporte mais limpo e justo.

Por fim, ela destacou a importância de quebrar a visão eurocêntrica no atletismo mundial, trazendo mais provas e reconhecimento para outras regiões, como a América do Sul. A presença de provas com selo no Brasil, como a La Misión, que conquistou o selo Ouro, é um passo importante. Natacha, como brasileira, ressaltou seu papel em levar uma perspectiva diferente para as decisões da federação, que historicamente foi muito centrada na Europa. Com o crescimento do esporte no Brasil, ela acredita no potencial do país para, futuramente, sediar campeonatos mundiais.
